extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate or beginning graduate students studying algebraic topology (readers of the textbook)
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, constructions, and basic properties of simplicial and singular homology: chain groups, boundary maps, homology groups, functoriality, homotopy invariance, computations (examples), simplicial approximation, and the Lefschetz fixed point theorem. Targeted at students learning to compute and reason with homology for CW/Δ-complexes and general spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homology depends only on (n+1)-skeleton for CW complexes
rubrics_metrics.description: For a CW complex X, the homology group H_n(X) depends only on the (n+1)-skeleton of X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that homology is low-dimensional in nature in the sense homology groups for CW complexes are determined by finitely many skeleton layers; motivates cellular homology and computability advantages over higher homotopy groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chain groups are free abelian on n-cells / n-simplices
rubrics_metrics.description: For a cell complex (or Δ-complex) X, C_n(X) is the free abelian group with basis the n cells (open n-simplices) of X; for singular homology, C_n(X) is free abelian on all singular n-simplices σ: Δ^n → X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chains are finite formal Z-linear combinations of basis simplices; in simplicial (Δ-) complexes the basis is the combinatorial simplices, while in singular homology the basis is (typically uncountably many) continuous maps of standard simplices into X.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boundary homomorphism and orientation rule for simplices
rubrics_metrics.description: Boundary ∂_n on an ordered simplex [v0,...,vn] is ∂[v0,...,vn] = Σ_i (-1)^i [v0,...,hat{v_i},...,vn]; the ordering of vertices determines orientations of faces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Δ-complexes vertices of faces are ordered according to their order in the larger simplex; signs account for coherent orientations. This rule generalizes to singular simplices via restriction to faces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chain complex condition: ∂∘∂ = 0
rubrics_metrics.description: For the sequence of boundary homomorphisms ... → C_{n+1} --∂_{n+1}→ C_n --∂_n→ C_{n-1} → ..., one has ∂_n ∂_{n+1} = 0 for each n (equivalently Im ∂_{n+1} ⊂ Ker ∂_n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This algebraic condition (proved for simplicial and singular boundaries) is essential so that boundaries are cycles and the homology quotient Ker ∂_n / Im ∂_{n+1} is well-defined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of homology groups H_n
rubrics_metrics.description: The n-th homology group of a chain complex is H_n = Ker ∂_n / Im ∂_{n+1}; for a space X with chain groups C_n(X), H_n(X) = Ker ∂_n / Im ∂_{n+1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cycles are elements of Ker ∂_n, boundaries are elements of Im ∂_{n+1}; homology classes are cosets of boundaries. Examples (graphs, torus, RP^2, spheres) illustrate geometric meaning: H_1 counts 1-dimensional 'holes', H_2 counts enclosed 3D-type holes, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicial homology setup for Δ-complexes (D–complexes)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Δ-complex (called D–complex here) structure consists of characteristic maps σ_α: Δ^n → X satisfying (i) each σ_α|_{int Δ^n} is injective and each point of X lies in exactly one such interior, (ii) restrictions to faces match other characteristic maps via canonical linear homeomorphisms preserving vertex order, (iii) topology condition: A ⊂ X is open iff preimages under all σ_α are open.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This defines the combinatorial domain for simplicial homology; permits building X as quotient of disjoint simplices and ensures X is Hausdorff and that open simplices are images of interiors of standard simplices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicial boundary maps defined on characteristic maps
rubrics_metrics.description: For a Δ-complex, define ∂_n(σ_α) = Σ_i (-1)^i σ_α|[v0,...,hat{v_i},...,vn], and extend linearly to obtain ∂_n: C_n(X) → C_{n-1}(X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The right side lies in C_{n-1}(X) since restrictions to faces are characteristic maps of (n-1)-simplices; this yields the simplicial chain complex and homology H_n^Δ(X).

rubrics_metrics.name: Singular homology: definitions using all continuous maps of simplices
rubrics_metrics.description: A singular n-simplex in X is any continuous map σ: Δ^n → X. Let C_n(X) be the free abelian group on singular n-simplices; define boundary by the same alternating-face formula. Then singular homology H_n(X) = Ker ∂_n / Im ∂_{n+1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Singular homology is defined for all topological spaces (not just Δ-complexes); singular chain groups are usually very large but the resulting homology groups are often manageable. For Δ-complexes singular homology coincides with simplicial homology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functoriality: maps induce chain maps and homomorphisms on homology
rubrics_metrics.description: A continuous map f: X → Y induces f_#: C_n(X) → C_n(Y) by composition f_#(σ) = f ∘ σ; f_# is a chain map satisfying f_# ∂ = ∂ f_#, hence induces f_*: H_n(X) → H_n(Y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Properties include (f ∘ g)_* = f_* ∘ g_* and id_* = id. This functoriality is used for computing, comparing homology, and proving invariance results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homotopy invariance of homology
rubrics_metrics.description: If two maps f, g: X → Y are homotopic, then they induce the same homomorphism f_* = g_*: H_n(X) → H_n(Y). Consequently, a homotopy equivalence f: X → Y induces isomorphisms f_*: H_n(X) → H_n(Y) for all n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses subdivision of Δ^n × I into simplices and construction of chain homotopies; corollary: contractible spaces have trivial reduced homology in positive dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: H_0 characterization and splitting over path components
rubrics_metrics.description: For nonempty path-connected X, H_0(X) ≈ Z; in general H_0(X) is a direct sum of Z's, one for each path component. More generally, H_n(X) ≈ ⊕_α H_n(X_α) for decomposition into path-components X_α.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses the augmentation ε: C_0(X) → Z (sum of coefficients) and shows Ker ε = Im ∂_1 when X is path-connected; useful for interpreting H_0 as counting components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduced homology and augmentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Augment the chain complex with ε: C_0(X) → Z to define reduced homology groups ẐH_n(X) so that a point has trivial homology in all dimensions including n=0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires X nonempty; the augmentation induces H_0(X) ≈ ẐH_0(X) ⊕ Z and ẐH_n(X) ≈ H_n(X) for n > 0. Conceptually makes statements about all dimensions simpler (e.g., contractible ⇒ all reduced homology zero).

rubrics_metrics.name: Computational examples and geometric interpretation of homology classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: graphs (H_1 free abelian on cycles), torus T with H_1(T) ≈ Z⊕Z, H_2(T) ≈ Z, RP^2 homology computations showing torsion/index-two subgroup phenomena, S^n with homology Z in dimensions 0 and n and 0 otherwise (for simplicial model with two n-simplices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chain computations demonstrate how attaching cells (filling cycles) changes homology: attaching 2-cell along a cycle kills that 1-cycle in H_1; attaching 3-cell can kill a 2-cycle, etc. Examples illustrate how homology measures holes of different dimensions and how boundaries mod out cycles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Singular complex model equating singular and simplicial homology
rubrics_metrics.description: For any space X the singular complex S(X) (a Δ-complex with one n-simplex for each singular n-simplex σ: Δ^n→X) has simplicial homology identical to the singular homology H_n(X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This shows singular homology is a special case of simplicial homology, but the singular complex is usually extremely large compared to X; conceptually useful to relate theories and transfer results proven for simplicial homology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric realization of cycles via finite complexes
rubrics_metrics.description: A singular n-chain ξ = Σ ε_i σ_i (ε_i = ±1) can be represented by a finite Δ-complex K_ξ obtained by identifying faces corresponding to canceling (n−1)-faces; if ξ is a cycle, K_ξ is manifold-like away from low-dimensional skeleton and induces a map K_ξ → X representing the homology class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: elements of H_1(X) are represented by oriented loops; elements of H_2(X) by maps of closed oriented surfaces; cycles that are boundaries correspond to extending the map to a manifold with boundary. This gives geometric intuition for homology classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicial approximation theorem and simplicial approximation conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a continuous map f: |K| → |L| between simplicial complexes, after sufficient barycentric subdivision of K there exists a simplicial map g homotopic to f with the property that for each vertex v of subdivided K, f(st(v)) ⊂ st(g(v)) (the star condition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The simplicial approximation can be chosen stationary on vertices already sent to vertices by f, and can be made arbitrarily close by subdividing both domain and target. Used to replace continuous maps by combinatorial (simplicial) ones for computations and constructions (e.g., proving homotopy equivalences, mapping cones).

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicial approximation applied to CW complexes (existence of simplicial models)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every CW complex X is homotopy equivalent to a simplicial complex Y of the same dimension (finite if X finite, countable if X countable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses simplicial approximation on attaching maps and constructs simplicial analogs of mapping cylinders and cones; permits treating CW complexes combinatorially for homotopy-theoretic arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lefschetz number and fixed point criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: For a map f: X → X of a finite CW complex (or more generally a space whose homology groups are finitely generated and vanish in high dimensions), the Lefschetz number is τ(f) = Σ_n (-1)^n tr(f_*: H_n(X) → H_n(X)). If X is a finite simplicial complex (or retract of one) and τ(f) ≠ 0 then f has a fixed point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: τ is homotopy invariant; if f has no fixed points one can find a simplicial approximation g homotopic to f with g(σ) ∩ σ = ∅ for all simplices σ, forcing diagonal entries of induced chain maps to be zero and hence τ(f)=0. Apply to projective spaces, spheres, etc., to deduce existence/nonexistence of fixed points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trace additivity and computation of τ(f) via cellular chain complexes
rubrics_metrics.description: The trace of an endomorphism on a short exact sequence splits additively (tr β = tr α + tr γ). For a simplicial map g respecting skeleta, τ(g) can be computed as Σ_n (-1)^n tr(g_*: H_n(K_n, K_{n-1}) → H_n(K_n, K_{n-1})).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in Lefschetz theorem proofs: if g(σ) ∩ σ = ∅ for each n-simplex then diagonal entries vanish so corresponding trace is 0. Algebraic reduction involves factoring torsion and reducing to free cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mayer–Vietoris and cellular homology as computational tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Mayer–Vietoris sequences and cellular homology are presented as powerful techniques for efficient computation of homology groups (cellular homology is ‘homology squared’: homology defined in terms of homology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mayer–Vietoris is the homology analog of van Kampen for π1; cellular homology reduces computations to cellular chain complexes determined by CW-structure and cellular boundary maps (developed later in chapter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiomatic characterization of homology for CW complexes
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist algebraic axioms (listed later in the chapter) which completely characterize homology groups for CW complexes; one may treat homology abstractly by these axioms rather than by geometric definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text postpones axioms until the theory is established; viewpoint: axioms (Eilenberg–Steenrod-type) capture the essential algebraic content of homology and show uniqueness/existence up to natural isomorphism for CW complexes.
